case.statement: The archive's account extends the field's ontology. Its definitions take Pessoa's own distinction and typology as their ground (the 1928 note and the Casais Monteiro letter, both in the field as F39, F16, F10) and add senses on the field's own object: the heteronym as function and position, the extended typology, ethics and disclosure, the meta-heteronym, the cross-substrate category, the analytic heteronym applied to antiquity, and measured findings on the documented corpora. Its strongest contests (Pessoa formalized rather than invented; a heteronym is a person) have counterparts in the field (B3's Yeats-as-originator, F26, F31; B3's 'a real man ... except one, which is being real itself', F27), so the law of the suppressed witness does not apply (§0.10: not where the field holds the ontology, however marginally). The margin is recorded: the cross-substrate heteronym and the analytic heteronym in antiquity are senses no field source supplies, but the defining papers state them as extensions of the same typology, not as a rival ontology of the heteronym, so the row is composed as equal, not mixed.

loci.quote: This document formalizes the typology of authorial voices operative in Fernando Pessoa's heteronymic system and offers an extension of that typology adequate to contemporary heteronymic practice and knowledge-graph representation.
These three categories are Pessoa's own and are thoroughly documented in his writings.
The document positions this latter development — here termed *The New Human* — as a theorizable extension of the heteronymic tradition.
The substrate dimension adds a new variable but does not violate the typological structure.
The meta-heteronym is not a discovery. It is a naming.
The proposal is to add to those modes of reading one more — typological — that allows us to see the Pessoa archive as an operative piece within a broader genre of heteronymic technologies.
The practice is not new. What is new is the naming.
It is crucial to mark that this is an analytic category, not a claim about historical self-description.
The definition employed here owes its modern articulation to Fernando Pessoa's correspondence with Adolfo Casais Monteiro (January 13, 1935)
This is not a novel claim. It is the claim Pessoa made in 1914 and maintained until his death in 1935.

E_F.type: C (public entity: a literary concept and practice)
E_F.definition: one or more imaginary characters a writer creates to write in different styles, with their own supposed physiques, biographies and writing styles, distinguished from pseudonyms (false names); named and developed by Pessoa in the early twentieth century, explored earlier by Kierkegaard (B1–B8)

E_A.definition: a named authorial function or position that a compositional system constitutes and sustains: not a pseudonym, which changes the label, but a change in the organization of the authorial function, with its own biography, poetics, lineage and voice, writing from a constructed position; attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to it, and ethical only under stated conditions; in a system, an architecture of positions (orthonym, heteronym, semi-, proto-, para-heteronym) of which Pessoa is the canonical case and not the origin

rho.statement: the archive reads E_F as the entity: it takes Pessoa's own distinction and typology as its ground and adds senses on the field's object (function and position; the extended typology; ethics and disclosure; the meta-heteronym; the cross-substrate and analytic extensions; measured findings on the documented corpora), each with the limits it states
rho.guard: ρ = extends claims an addition and no more. Where an archive sense contradicts a field claim, both are composed under P_coh in the one claim space: origin (F3, F25 against N96-01, N940-14); Kierkegaard (F11 against N666-04, N667-08, N940-09); Yeats (F31 against N667-11, N666-05); character or person (F1, F27 against N96-02); gimmick or technology (F44 against N682-04). The archive's own disagreements are composed as disagreements: person/position (N96-02, N90-02, N136-01), invented/formalized (N1127-02, N96-01), the meta-heteronym defined twice (N682-01, N666-07), the orthonym (N667-03, N123-08, N859-01, N1561-01).

KO.title: Literary heteronym
KO.genre: knowledge object composed under EA-NEGONT-02 v0.9 (#1690), equal-terms case: one claim space, the field's and the archive's claims ordered together by dependency and genealogy within each sense; nothing translated
KO.status: composed 2026-10-18 under v0.9; not frozen; ledgers unaudited (§3.8)

sentences.text: Pessoa drew the line himself: too radically different from him "to be considered simple pseudonyms", Richard Zenith writes in Literary Hub, his figures were called "heteronyms", and in a "Bibliographical Summary" of 1928, which Zenith and #96 both quote, Pessoa stated that "Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person", proceeding "from a full-fledged individual created by him, like the lines spoken by a character in a drama he might write"; the version the Poetry Society of America quotes makes the heteronymic work "the work of a complete individuality made up by him".

The field holds the line in the same terms: George Steiner (The Observer, 2001, quoted by Wikipedia) finds pseudonymous writing "not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance)", while heteronyms "as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange", and the Poetry Society account calls it "crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms".

Wikipedia defines the literary heteronym as "one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles", differing from pen names, "just false names", in being "characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles", as Art and Popular Culture also states it; Art and Soul Group calls them "fictitious authors" who "wrote" parts of Pessoa's work; a study in Studi Irlandesi adds world views and the capacity to hold "views in sharp contrast to those of the author who has created them", the heteronymic character presented as "a real man possessing human qualities like all other real men, except one, which is being real itself".

The archive's typology of Pessoa's system (#667) defines the pair as two literary operations: "A pseudonym is a name substitution", "while the writing remains that of the biographical person"; "A heteronym, in Pessoa's sense, is an independent authorial figure with its own biography, poetics, literary lineage, and voice — the writing emerges from a constructed position rather than from the biographical person behind the name"; collapsing them treats Pessoa's practice as "*elaborate pseudonym*", and #666 states heteronymic authorship as the biographical person writing "in a voice not their own, inhabiting an authorial position distinct from themselves".

Other deposits state the line from what the name does: "A pseudonym conceals identity. A heteronym creates it." (#1127); heteronyms are "other names that are also true" (#404); "A pseudonym may hide or rename an author. A heteronym creates a distinct authorial function." (#79); a heteronym "carries a full constructed biography, worldview, and stylistic signature; a pseudonym is a name without that structure" (#761); and #940 defines: "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.", its markers "testable", a pseudonymic operation failing "one or more", pseudonymy being where "the label changes but the function's organization does not".

The word has other senses: ThoughtCo notes that it "has multiple definitions, depending on its usage referring to grammar, its use in linguistics, or its use in literature", and #921 marks the Habermas–Jauss usage as "technically distinct from the literary practice of *heteronymy* — the production of distinct authorial identities by a single writer, in the lineage of Fernando Pessoa".

#348 and #79 define the heteronym as a function: within the archive's own framework, NH-OS, #348 holds that heteronyms "are not pseudonyms, masks, or personas" but "**authorial functions**", authorship treated "as a system, not a name"; for #79 a heteronym is "a structure-function: a sustained authorial position, internally coherent across style, method, domain, output, and bearing-cost", "validated not by declaration but by performance", "not a false name" but "a true function", and alias capture its opposite, attaching a claimant to an authority-bearing name "without performing the name's function" (#79).

#90 defines it as "a constitutional position — a structurally-defined location from which specific kinds of semantic labor are bearable"; #123, in an analytic sense, as "a stable authorial position that is operationally distinguishable from other authorial positions in the same project", "functionally required by an operation the project is performing" — "The heteronyms are not disguises; they are *operations*"; #794 as "the production of content under a name that is *not the producer's*, with the attributed entity possessing a constructed identity distinct from the producer's own"; and #832 holds that the "I" of a heteronym "is evidence that the heteronymic system includes biographical construction as part of its architecture".

On whether the function is a person the archive's deposits disagree: #96 states "A heteronym is a person.", and limits it, the unconscious heteronym "not a person in the ontological sense this essay defends" for lacking the consciousness "that makes heteronymic practice *practice*"; #90 says of the archive's own heteronyms that they "are not separate persons; they are differentiated positions"; and #136 reports as its parent paper's premise that "a heteronym must survive as a person, with biography, style, chronology, social relation, conflict, and plausible independence; otherwise it is not a heteronym but a transparent pseudonym"; on the mask the sources divide as well: for the Poetry Society account Pessoa's personae "were not so much disguises as extensions and iterations of himself"; #348 holds the heteronyms of NH-OS not masks; #666 that "A single heteronym is a mask; a system of heteronyms is an authorial architecture"; #852 that "The heteronym is a mask: it releases speech into open air".

Beside the heteronyms Wikipedia records two "whom Pessoa called semi-heteronyms, Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive", "semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality", in Pessoa's words to Casais Monteiro (13 January 1935) one whose personality, "although not my own, doesn't differ from my own but is a mere mutilation of it"; the Poetry Society account makes Soares "the closest identity to a pseudonym"; and "There is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, who also considers Caeiro his master", which Art and Soul Group glosses as "the "orthonym," that is, himself", from whom each heteronym is unlike in personality, biography and style.

#667 consolidates these as Pessoa's own categories, the orthonym defined as "The author's own name, but as literary voice — not as biographical person", with the proto-heteronym and para-heteronym by which "Teresa Rita Lopes and subsequent critics have extended the typology", the para-heteronym defined: "A second-order figure operating *within* the heteronymic system, typically as a translator, critic, or commentator on other heteronyms", and a strict heteronym test of five criteria (a distinct proper name; a fictional biography; a distinctive poetics in a substantial body of text; influences other than Pessoa's orthonymic poetics; documented reciprocal relations to other heteronyms); #666 argues that practice under other terminologies "should be recognized as heteronymic when it meets the typological criteria"; #668 finds these categories, "that Pessoa himself articulated", treated as undifferentiated by existing data infrastructure, collapsed into "pseudonym" or flattened "to "heteronym" (as Wikidata currently does)", Wikidata holding as of April 2026 "approximately twenty-five to thirty Pessoa-related items".

The orthonym is defined three further ways and the definitions do not coincide: #123 calls the position bearing "the legal-biological-civil identity of the writer" a definition "contingent on the modern legal-individualist apparatus" and gives "A stronger analytic definition": "the authorial position that bears the project's founding operative gesture, regardless of which substrate or legal identity that position occupies"; #165 makes the distinction one between "*the structural position of singular intent*" and "*the structural position of executory transmission*"; #859 defines the orthonym as "not the real name" but "the regulatory fiction that stabilizes a heteronymic system", Socrates "the central mask through which Plato's authorship is distributed"; on Pessoa's corpus #1561 records the conflict: "Under Pessoa's own usage the orthonym is the position bearing the civil name, which is Pessoa-himself"; under the functional definition it is "arguably Caeiro, the master the other voices acknowledge and organise themselves around"; the seat "records both readings and settles neither".

Pessoa described his enterprise, Poetry International records, as "a drama divided into people instead of into acts" — "the theatre of being" or "drama in people", in Wikipedia — and wrote, the Poetry Society quotes, "I break my soul into pieces," "and into different persons"; the process "began in Pessoa's childhood, gathered steam in his adolescence with the invention of alter egos who wrote in English, and made literary history in 1914" with Caeiro, Campos and Reis, works "over half of which were signed by one of three alter egos, all of whom came into being in 1914", as Zenith puts it; #682 reads the planned "drama em gente" among the acts by which Pessoa "can be read, without irony, as the first modern meta-heteronym", and reads *Orpheu* (1915) as "a meta-heteronymic institution".

Caeiro, Poetry International writes, "the first in the poetic trinity to emerge from Pessoa's soul, was considered the Master of the other two and, indeed, of Pessoa himself"; Wikipedia names him, Reis and Campos the three chief heteronyms, "the latter two consider the former their master", and Art and Soul Group calls Caeiro "the "master" of heteronyms"; #1570 finds that "Every term by which Caeiro is known is ABSENT from Caeiro", paganism, sensationism, objectivism, "*the master*" and sensibility "all supplied by Mora, Campos and Reis"; in Pessoa, #1572 finds, "**The master position is constituted by dying.**"; and #348 states, of heteronyms within NH-OS, that "The death of a heteronym is not failure. It is **formal completion**."

Wikipedia records that the heteronyms "criticise and translate each other's works" and that some "are relatives or know each other"; the Poetry Society account adds that they "collaborated on projects (Crosse worked with his brother, I. I. Crosse)", Poetry International that "There was considerable interaction among the heteronyms", and Steiner finds for each voice an idiom, a biography and "subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness"; #1570 reads master–student and heteronymic configuration as "not competing relation-types", a configuration able to "**itself instantiate**" a master–student relation, "**Pessoa is the existence proof**": "A single person can generate genuine asymmetry, inheritance, criticism, development, mastership, discipleship, stylistic separation, and differing conceptual commitments."; they "sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life": "a jealous Campos wrote letters to the girl" in Pessoa's only attested romance (Art and Popular Culture), and "The largest and most playful of the heteronyms" "even meddled in Pessoa's real-world life" (Poetry International).

The counts run by source and criterion: "at least 70" by "the latest count by Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes" (Wikipedia); "approximately seventy-two distinct authorial figures" by Lopes's archival work (#667); "about 75 different names" (Studi Irlandesi); "more than seventy personae" (Poetry Society); "over seventy heteronyms" (#1127); "twelve heteronyms, plus one" (#96); and for Zenith "more than one hundred fictitious authors" if the childhood riddlers and humorists are included, "About thirty" signing a significant work, "only three full-fledged heteronyms", the word used "rather loosely", "Authorized by Pessoa's example".

On origin the sources contradict one another: Wikipedia has heteronyms "named and developed" by Pessoa "in the early 20th century" but "thoroughly explored" by Kierkegaard "in the 19th century", who "Had more than a dozen heteronyms with distinct biographies and personalities"; the Studi Irlandesi study credits Pessoa with "the development, naming and introduction of this concept into literature"; #1127 calls him "the Portuguese poet who invented the form"; #96 holds "Fernando Pessoa did not invent heteronymic practice. He formalized it."; and #940, "The practice is not new. What is new is the naming."

#666 reads Pessoa's practice as "not a freak event in literary history but the canonical case of a describable theoretical practice", "Pessoa sits at its apex as the most richly and self-consciously theorized instance, but not as its origin or termination", and holds that Kierkegaard "operated heteronymically in substantively the same sense Pessoa later did, half a century earlier and without the term"; #667 maps Kierkegaard's pseudonymous authors "predominantly to the heteronym category in the extended sense", #940 calls the authorship "more properly heteronymous", and #123 finds Kierkegaard "arguably closer to the Socratic case than Pessoa" — against Steiner, for whom Kierkegaard is the celebrated instance of pseudonymous writing.

On Yeats the Studi Irlandesi study holds, as hypothesis, that "strong heteronymic qualities can also be discerned" in works "some of which produced about twenty years before Pessoa even started his career", finds "three fictional names; Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne, Michael Robartes", and concludes that "Yeats either originated the concept, albeit without giving it a name, or paved the way", or "could have been a source of inspiration and influence for Pessoa"; Zenith finds "some faint parallels", Yeats's Robartes and Owen Hearne "a duo of "collaborators" with contrasting personalities" and Machado's Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín; #667 places Robartes and Hearne as "occupying a zone between heteronym and literary character", #666 calls them "partial heteronyms", "more developed than pseudonyms, less developed than Pessoa's chief heteronyms", #667 holds Mairena and Martín "heteronymic figures in substantially Pessoan sense" and Borges's Menard "typologically distinct", "a diegetic character with an extradiegetic theoretical function".

The archive draws the lineage further: #1560 seats Browning, Pound and Pessoa as "one practice at three stages of its development", Pound "the middle term, where the mask stops being a character in a poem and becomes a position the poet inhabits"; #263 places the Crimson Hexagon "In the tradition of Browning's and Pound's *Personae*, and approaching Fernando Pessoa's art of the heteronym"; #68's doctrine of the Secret Name names heteronymic practice "a 5,000-year technology for creating new persons through naming", and #96 records its encoding as "a continuous tradition from Pharaonic Titulary (~2600 BCE) through Pessoa to the present day".

Readings of the practice differ: Gaspar Simões, Zenith reports, read it "through a Freudian lens" and "deemed them symptomatic of the author's inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in the act of writing", "a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick"; the Poetry Society account holds that the conceit "didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention", that the selves "were instruments of exorcism and redemption" (Zenith), and that "no one took the ruse as far as Pessoa did—and certainly no one has since"; Zenith holds that "Pessoa staked his very identity on the heteronymous system" and that "no writer can rival" his "glorious if not always harmonious musical ensemble".

#682 states as its central thesis "heteronymy is a technology, not a pathology", holding that Pessoa criticism, "in reading heteronymy primarily through psychology, sensation, or phenomenology, has left open" "the institutional-architectural dimension"; #584 names "the Pessoa reading" as "heteronymy as literary technique, productive, interesting, ultimately aesthetic"; for #1569 heteronymy "on this logic, converts κερματισμός from a wound into a method"; #1658 as "a tool for dividing a mind so that it can make".

#682 defines the meta-heteronym as "a heteronymic system whose personae do not only produce literary works, but the institutional apparatus itself (introductions, criticism, historiography, bibliography) under which those works become legible", its five conditions "necessary together", "A pseudonymous system satisfying C1 but not C2 (Kierkegaard in part) is merely multi-pseudonymous"; it holds that "A hoax is a meta-heteronym that depends on non-disclosure", and limits the reading: "This reading is typological, not causal. It does not claim Pessoa "anticipated" digital infrastructure."; #666 defines the meta-heteronym otherwise, "an inscription that generates heteronyms", and holds, as hypothesis, that heteronyms "may have lives beyond their originating author".

#940 defines heteronymy as "the ethical practice of sustaining a distinct named authorial function without falsely reducing it to a civil identity, and without falsely presenting it as an independent civil person", the authorial function "attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer", and gives the working definition: heteronymy "occurs when a compositional system deliberately constitutes and sustains a named authorial function that is neither identical with nor reducible to the civil bearer, while preserving truthful provenance about the substrates and responsibilities through which that function operates", reading the Caesar/God distinction as "applicable at the authorial layer".

Its limits are #940's own: "Heteronymy is not ethical by its existence. It can also be used to deceive, evade responsibility, fabricate consensus, impersonate independent persons, or multiply one voice into false corroboration"; "False multiplication of the same voice into apparent independent corroboration is not heteronymy in the ethical sense. It is fabrication."; and the deposit's agreement with its own practice "is not, however, verification".

On disclosure #96 holds that "The entire system depends on the practitioner's *consciousness* of the construction"; #1569 finds that both documented heteronymic corpora "announced themselves in print, and those announcements are the **only reason the groupings are known**", so that "A criterion that treats declaration as disqualifying classifies both documented heteronymic corpora as non-heteronymic", and corrects it: "a declaration disqualifies only if it would have been read, at the time, as revealing heteronymic construction".

Outside literature Wikipedia lists David Bowie, who "Systematically employed heteronyms as a performer"; #682 holds that "An Instagram profile is a heteronym"; #96 holds, as hypothesis, that "Facebook turned the *orthonym itself* into a heteronym" "at civilizational scale, without the practitioner's knowledge or consent"; #794 reads an account whose producers "are not concealing their identity (OCEARCH openly manages the account)", attributing content "to an entity that cannot produce content", as "heteronymy in the precise Pessoan sense, extended to the institutional-zoological domain", the non-human attributed case #940 includes "as an experimental edge case rather than as central proof".

#667 introduces "a tentative category — *cross-substrate heteronym*"; #666 states the practice novel, with "no nineteenth- or early-twentieth-century equivalent, because the substrates did not exist", and adds "This is not to claim that Pessoa practiced cross-substrate heteronymy — he did not, and could not."; #667 claims for its typology "adequacy to the practices it was developed to describe", not "cultural universality", and states that classical, certain non-European and oral literatures "may require adjustments the PKG has not yet made".

#123 proposes, as hypothesis, that "the foundational corpus of Western philosophy *can be read as* a single distributed authorial project rather than only as three independent authorships", marks "that this is an analytic category, not a claim about historical self-description", disclaims that "Pessoa-style or CHA-style heteronymy existed as a named or institutionalized practice in classical Athens", offers the archive "as *availability of concept*" and "not as evidence", names "the biological-individuation model of authorship" as the assumption that obscured the configuration, and keeps "the weaker, more defensible" claim: the reading "becomes *thinkable*" and "is not *proven*".

#123 separates pseudepigrapha, which involve "*concealment*: a text is attributed to a figure who did not write it, in order to acquire that figure's authority"; #68 lists an "**Inherited**" named position, "a disciple writes under a teacher's name", the Pauline school among its cases, a "**Split**" one, "one person occupies multiple positions (Pessoa's system; the Dodecad)", and the "**Heteronymic**", "a created name functioning independently"; #203 proposes, as hypothesis, the New Testament authors as "heteronymic author-functions within the Josephan literary system", with its falsifier, the theory "shown to be inapplicable to ancient texts"; and #940 treats Christian transmission as "a heteronymic structure".

#136 states a No-Floor Theorem — under the premise that documentary separateness is constructed by a heteronymic configuration, "the heteronymic method possesses no criterion, internal to itself, for halting the attribution of any adjacent named figure to the configuration" — and reads it: "*it is not a method for discovering identities. It is a method for revealing functional structure.*"; its firewall, "Biographical identity requires evidence. Functional identity requires pattern."; its primary claim, as hypothesis, that institutional scholarship "cannot distinguish ordinary multi-author transmission from mature heteronymic construction using the instruments it currently relies on"; its limit, "*the paper does not assert that the founding corpus was written by one hidden person.*", and "*a configuration may function as a symbolon whether or not it was struck as one*"; #1562, of a two-part Kierkegaard work, finds that "the fit is not stated anywhere inside either half. That is the shape a heteronymic configuration takes".

#1658, later and as hypothesis, names "one self-dividing maker" as the production model the Platonic, Theophrastan and Aristotelian corpus is consistent with, "nothing in it" requiring "another maker" — the maximal form #136 does not assert.

#1560 takes Pessoa, whose letter to Casais Monteiro of 13 January 1935 "attributes the heteronyms, so the grouping is known rather than inferred", as "the positive control for any instrument claiming to detect designed differentiation", and #1562 Kierkegaard as "the second calibration case", who "acknowledged the pseudonymous authorship in print" in 1846 and 1851; #1570 records both as "one-name-one-voice by construction" (Victor Eremita excepted) and Pessoa's minor heteronyms as "unavailable", pt.wikisource carrying "only Caeiro, Reis, Campos and the orthonym".

On these corpora #1570 measures that "Pooling the three heteronyms recovers the orthonym at **0.0258** — inside the M1 same-author band", the best single heteronym Campos at 0.0498 — "Individually the voices do not look like Pessoa; summed, they do.", with a size confound, shaky cross-language comparison and four of about twelve Kierkegaard pseudonymous works seated among its stated limits; and that the reception capture it found on Caeiro "is NOT DISTINCTIVE of heteronymy", occurring "in both classes".
Of the instruments, #1572 finds that "**Relation-type is not recoverable from lexical distribution** — not pupillage, not constructed lineage, not heteronymic construction".

The heteronymic architectures are not one (#1572): "PESSOA CLOSES BY REMAINDER; THE CONFIGURATION WOULD CLOSE BY SUM", a heteronymic series being, as #1571 hypothesizes, "a search downward" in which "Each position subtracts something and tests whether a voice survives the subtraction"; and #1572 limits it: "Two of the best-documented heteronymists built the Socratic structure, and imitation cannot be distinguished from convergence on the cases available."

P.title: Literary heteronym
P.genre: the compression: AIO's interaction grammar (lede, headed clusters, bolded labels), composed from the same plan as the KO in one claim space (v0.9 §4.8, §5.8)

lede.text: is an authorial figure a writer creates and writes as, unlike the pseudonym, a false name: in Pessoa's 1928 words, "heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person" (Zenith; #96). It has its own supposed physique, biography and style (Wikipedia), and is an authorial function, attributable through its civil bearer and not reducible to it (#940).

items.label: Definition:
items.text: a character with its own physique, biography and style (Wikipedia), writing from a constructed position (#667).

items.label: The line:
items.text: pseudonymous writing "not rare", heteronyms "exceedingly strange" (Steiner); a pseudonym changes the label, a heteronym the function's organization (#940).

items.label: Function:
items.text: within NH-OS, "not pseudonyms, masks, or personas" (#348); a structure-function validated by performance (#79).

items.label: Person or position:
items.text: "a person" (#96); "differentiated positions" (#90); one heteronym a mask, a system an architecture (#666).

items.label: Positions:
items.text: orthonym, heteronym, semi-heteronym (Wikipedia); proto- and para-heteronym (Lopes and later critics, #667).
Caeiro, Reis, Campos; Caeiro "the Master" (Poetry International), his epithets supplied by the others (#1570).

items.label: Interplay:
items.text: they criticise, translate and meddle in Pessoa's life (Wikipedia; Poetry International); one maker can build master and disciples (#1570).

items.label: Counts:
items.text: at least 70 (Lopes), about 72 (#667), about 75 (Studi Irlandesi), over 100 with childhood figures (Zenith); "only three full-fledged".

items.label: Orthonym:
items.text: civil name, or founding gesture, "arguably Caeiro"; unsettled (#1561).

items.label: Invented?
items.text: "named and developed" by Pessoa (Wikipedia); formalized, not invented (#96).

items.label: Kierkegaard:
items.text: a pseudonymist (Steiner), or heteronymic half a century early (#666).

items.label: Yeats:
items.text: originator or precursor (Studi Irlandesi, hypothesis); partial heteronyms (#666); between heteronym and character (#667).

items.label: A history:
items.text: Pessoa its apex, not its origin (#666); Browning, Pound, Pessoa (#1560).

items.label: Gimmick or technology:
items.text: "subterfuge" (Gaspar Simões, via Zenith); "technology, not a pathology" (#682).

items.label: Meta-heteronym:
items.text: personae that produce their own reception apparatus; typological, not causal (#682).

items.label: Ethics:
items.text: no reduction to a civil name, no false independence; "not ethical by its existence" (#940); declared in print, both documented cases (#1569).

items.label: Further:
items.text: Bowie (Wikipedia); a tentative cross-substrate heteronym (#667); antiquity, thinkable, not proven (#123).

items.label: Summed:
items.text: pooled, the heteronyms recover the orthonym; size-confounded, by its own limits (#1570).

items.label: Not decisive:
items.text: capture occurs in both classes (#1570); relation-type is not recoverable from lexical distribution (#1572).

open.question: Is a heteronym a person or a position?
open.modality: stipulation (#96, #90, #348 within NH-OS, #123 analytic), attributed (#136), stipulation (F27); contested within the archive
open.would_resolve: a deposit that states which definition the archive holds, or an operator ruling

open.question: Which voice is Pessoa's orthonym?
open.would_resolve: an instrument that determines the orthonym rather than assumes it, as #1561 states, calibrated on Pessoa as the positive control (#1560)

open.question: Did Pessoa invent the heteronym, name it, or formalize it?
open.modality: documented, attributed and hypothesis (field); documented (#1127), interpretation (#96), self-description (#940)
open.would_resolve: dated pre-Pessoan practice meeting #667's strict heteronym test

open.question: Are Kierkegaard's authors pseudonyms or heteronyms?
open.modality: attributed and documented (field); interpretation and stipulation (archive)
open.would_resolve: Kierkegaard's pseudonyms scored on #667's strict test and #682's five conditions

open.question: Does the typology reach beyond the practices it was built on?

translation.received: "Too radically different from him to be considered simple pseudonyms, as if only their names had changed, Pessoa called them “heteronyms,”" (B6, ¶3); "in a “Bibliographical Summary” of his works published in 1928 he explained the conceptual distinction: “Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person. They proceed from a full-fledged individual created by him, like the lines spoken by a character in a drama he might write.”" (B6, ¶3 (Bibliographical Summary, 1928)); "A pseudonymic work is, except for the name with which it is signed, the work of an author writing as himself; a heteronymic work is by an author writing outside his own personality: it is the work of a complete individuality made up by him, just as the utterances of some character in a drama of his would be." (B2, body (Pessoa quoted)); "Pseudonymous writing is not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance). 'Heteronyms', as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange." (B1, George Steiner on the heteronyms); "It is crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms." (B2, body); "George Steiner, "A man of many parts", in The Observer, Sunday, 3 June 2001." (B1, George Steiner on the heteronyms (source line))

translation.received: "The literary concept of the heteronym refers to one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles." (B1, lead ¶1); "Heteronyms differ from pen names (or pseudonyms, from the Greek words for "fake" and "name") in that the latter are just false names, while the former are characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles." (B1, lead ¶1); "The literary concept of heteronym, invented by Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa, refers to one or more imaginary character(s) created by a poet to write in different styles." (B4, article ¶1); "Heteronyms differ from nom de plumes (or pseudonyms, from the Greek "False Name") in that the latter are just false names, while the former are characters having their own supposed physiques, biographies and writing styles." (B4, article ¶1); "Pessoa left his mark as an extremely original writer for inventing fictitious authors – heteronyms – who “wrote” parts of his work." (B5, opening); "However, unlike pseudonyms, heteronyms are names given to fully developed characters that, in spite of being imaginary, possess nearly all human qualities such as physical features, biographies, world views, writing styles, etc. – characters that, surprisingly enough, are capable of having views in sharp contrast to those of the author who has created them." (B3, abstract); "In spite of being created by the writer himself, a heteronymic character is presented in such a way that the readers consider him as a completely distinct figure, a real man possessing human qualities like all other real men, except one, which is being real itself." (B3, §1 Introduction)

translation.received: "The heteronyms dialogue with each other and even with Pessoa in what he calls "the theatre of being" or "drama in people"." (B1, Pessoa's heteronyms ¶2); ""I break my soul into pieces," he wrote, "and into different persons."" (B2, body); "Fernando Pessoa (1888-1935), describing his literary enterprise as “a drama divided into people instead of into acts”, split himself into dozens of dramatis personae, the “heteronyms”, who occupied the stage of his otherwise uneventful life." (B8, ¶1); "It was a process that began in Pessoa’s childhood, gathered steam in his adolescence with the invention of alter egos who wrote in English, and made literary history in 1914, with the creation of would-be shepherd Alberto Caeiro, Futurist naval engineer Álvaro de Campos, and classicist Ricardo Reis, three of the finest Portuguese poets of the twentieth century." (B8, ¶1); "over half of which were signed by one of three alter egos, all of whom came into being in 1914, shortly before the outbreak of World War I." (B6, ¶2); "Pessoa's dozens of constructed alternate selves, Zenith noted, "were instruments of exorcism and redemption." (B2, body)

Yeats (1865-1939), strong heteronymic qualities can also be discerned in a number of his works some of which produced about twenty years before Pessoa even started his career as a writer." (B3, abstract); "Scanning the collected poems of Yeats, one comes across three fictional names; Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne, Michael Robartes." (B3, §1 Introduction); "Even if Pessoa did not borrow from Yeats in creating the concept of heteronym, it is still feasible to think that the heteronymic nature of Yeats’s works could have been a source of inspiration and influence for Pessoa." (B3, §5 Conclusion); "Thus, Yeats either originated the concept, albeit without giving it a name, or paved the way for its introduction into the Western literature that led Pessoa to his important achievement of heteronymic writings" (B3, §5 Conclusion); "The history of literature contains some faint parallels to his performance of multiple authorship. William Butler Yeats created Michael Robartes and Owen Hearne, a duo of “collaborators” with contrasting personalities." (B6, Rimbaud paragraph); "The Spanish poet Antonio Machado (1875–1939) also signed some of his poems and prose pieces with the names of two alter egos: Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín, who was Mairena’s “master.”" (B6, Rimbaud paragraph)

translation.received: "His heteronymic conceit didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention." (B2, body); "Although alter egos had become fashionable accessories for European writers in the early twentieth century, no one took the ruse as far as Pessoa did—and certainly no one has since." (B2, body); "But no writer can rival Pessoa’s achievement of configuring, through his heteronyms, radically different poetic and philosophical attitudes that formed a glorious if not always harmonious musical ensemble." (B6, Rimbaud paragraph); "Gaspar Simões also discussed Pessoa’s literary work, viewing it through a Freudian lens, and devoted separate chapters to each of the three heteronyms. Despite admiring their poetry, he deemed them symptomatic of the author’s inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in the act of writing. The heteronyms, in his view, were a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick." (B6, Gaspar Simões paragraph)
